**On Time**

Time is a curious thing. It moves in only one direction, or so we believe, yet it pools in memory, stretches in boredom, and compresses in joy. We measure it with atomic precision—cesium-133 atoms oscillating 9,192,631,770 times per second define a single second—yet we experience it as something far more fluid, subjective, and often elusive.

Think of a childhood summer. As a child, those three months felt like an eternity, a landscape of endless possibility. The days stretched long, filled with the smell of cut grass and the drone of cicadas. As an adult, a summer can vanish in a blink, a blur of weekends and obligations. The same objective duration—roughly 90 days—undergoes a profound subjective metamorphosis. Neuroscientists suggest this is tied to novelty. For a child, nearly every day is new, etched deeply into memory. For an adult, routine blurs the days together. Our perception of time is, in a way, a byproduct of how much we notice.

This leads to a beautiful, melancholy truth: to make time feel fuller, we must fill it with attention. A mindful walk, where you notice the texture of bark on a tree or the pattern of clouds, can feel longer and richer than a distracted week spent scrolling through a digital feed. In our hyper-connected age, we have conquered space but often surrender time. We can speak to anyone across the globe instantly, yet we feel we never have “enough” time. Perhaps the issue isn’t the quantity of time, but the quality of our presence within it.

History gives us another lens. We live on a thin crust of the present, atop a deep, layered past. The ground beneath your feet holds fossils of ancient life, ruins of forgotten empires, the discarded objects of a thousand generations. Every place is a palimpsest. The street you walk on was once a riverbed, then a footpath, then a cobblestone road, now asphalt. Time is the great artist and eraser, constantly painting over its own work. We are merely the latest layer, and one day, we too will be a faint impression for some future being to puzzle over.

And then there’s the future, that great unknown. It exerts a constant gravitational pull on the present. We plan, we worry, we hope. Our lives are lived in a state of constant projection. This is, in many ways, our species’ superpower. The ability to simulate possible futures allowed us to survive as a fragile, slow, clawless creature on a planet full of sharper, faster predators. We could anticipate winter and store food, imagine a tool and create it. Yet this gift is also a burden. We can become so obsessed with the future—what might be, what we should achieve—that we forget to inhabit the now. The future is a useful map, but it is not the territory of your life. The territory is this breath, this sound, this moment of reading these words.

Cultures have different relationships with time. The Western, industrial model is largely linear: time is a resource, a commodity to be “spent,” “saved,” “wasted,” or “managed.” We talk about timelines, deadlines, and time-outs. It’s a highway, and the goal is to get as far down it as possible, as efficiently as possible.

Other cultures embrace a more cyclical view. Time is a wheel of seasons, harvests, festivals, and generations. It repeats. It is not a line to race along, but a rhythm to move with. This isn’t about being “on time” or “ahead of time,” but about being in time, in sync with larger natural and communal patterns. Neither view is wholly right or wrong; they are different ways of navigating existence. But it’s worth questioning the default setting we’ve adopted. Does treating time as a scarce resource to be optimized leave us feeling perpetually impoverished?

Physics, of course, adds another layer of wonder and confusion. Einstein showed us that time is relative. It bends and warps with gravity and speed. A clock on a satellite ticks slightly faster than one on the ground. Two synchronized watches can fall out of sync simply by traveling at different velocities. At the speed of light, time theoretically stops. This shatters our intuitive, everyday experience. Time is not the universal, steady metronome we thought. It is a local phenomenon, a feature of the observer’s journey through spacetime.

So, what is time? Is it the relentless, impartial force that turns mountains to dust? Is it the felt texture of our lives, elastic and subjective? Is it a river we float upon, or a cycle we dance within? Perhaps it is all of these, and more. It is the canvas upon which all stories are painted, the silent partner in every memory, the one thing we all share and yet experience utterly alone.

In the end, our relationship with time is one of the most fundamental of our lives. We cannot stop it, reverse it, or truly save it. But we can choose how we inhabit it. We can strive to be more present, to notice the light changing, to listen fully, to create moments of depth that will stand out against the blur. We can recognize that the present moment—this fragile, fleeting now—is the only one we ever truly possess. It is, in a way, the only real time there is. Everything else is either a memory or a dream. And so, the most profound act might not be to conquer time, but to meet it with open eyes, a grateful heart, and the courage to be here, now, as it unfolds.
